Centerville, Sept. 5. The opening of the republican campaign in Iowa was made here this afternoon. Hon. A. J. Cummins addressing a large audience of the people of Centerville and Appanoose county. In his speech Mr. Cummins treated all the issues, state and national, exhaustively. The tariff and our foreign policy, particularly as concerns the Philippines, were dwelt upon at length, and he did not mince matters in respect to state issues. Mr. Cummins presented, in an exceptionally able manner, the arguments to sustain the platform adopted at Cedar Rapids, and his words will be accepted as the keynote in the Iowa campaign. He referred briefly to the silver question, giving his reasons therefor, and although this may be said to be a dead issue, this part of his address must prove interesting. In brief, Mr. Cummins declared for a revision of the tariff and so adjusting the duty upon any commodity which is found to be substantially monopolized, that the tariff cannot be used to effect or perpetuate the monopoly.

In splendid presentation of all the phases of the Philippine question Mr. Cummins declared, without describing the particular tie that may ultimately bind the islands to the United States, that we may be absolutely certain that so long as the people of the United States continue to love liberty, have faith in free institutions, and are moved by virtuous impulses, whatever the relation between us and the races of the Philippine group ought to be, that it will be. Passing from the moral to the phase of the question, he said that so long as we are struggling with Europe for place in the commerce of China, there will be American territory in the Philippine islands and American harbors along their shores.

Mr. Cummins' mental attitude toward the democracy of Iowa is most considerate, but his treatment of the enormities of their platform was scathing and severe. Respecting the reiterated demand for the free and unlimited coinage of silver, he said there is a menace in it which should not be misunderstood. He believes the executive council when fixing the assessment of railways to be acting as a judicial body, and as he expects to become a member of that body, naturally did not state definitely what should be done in advance of the hearing. He did say, however, that a portion of property concealed from the assessor should be forfeited to the state, unless a better plan can be devised for reaching property which now remains invisible, that railroad companies cannot complain if they are compelled to pay taxes upon a valuation which puts them upon an equality with the owners of lands and lots; that authority to determine the value of property is lodged in the executive council, and finally, that if the people believe he has intelligence enough to ascertain what the value of railroad property is and courage enough to declare it, then he is entitled to their confidence and support. Mr. Cummins' preface to his regular address was non-partisan and contained much which should find place in the democratic as well as the republican literature of this campaign. He said:

"My Fellow Citizens: In the ancient days, when every man administered justice for himself and preserved his own safety as best he could, it required a great deal of his time and all his strength to maintain his rights and to keep his head firmly on his shoulders. In these modern days, when elaborate organized governments have been substituted to accomplish these purposes, it still requires much time, much thought, great virtue and high courage on the part of the voter to secure just laws and their honest execution. The more complex society becomes the more difficult the adjustment of government, and regulations will be, and each recurring year will demand higher intelligence, purer patriotism and more thoughtful attention at the hands of the citizens of this republic. The Alabama Polytechnic Institute, formerly called the Agricultural and Mechanical College, shall be under the superintendence and control of a board of trustees, which shall consist of two members from the Congressional District in which the Institute is located, and one each of the other Congressional Districts in this State; said trustees shall be appointed by the Governor, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, and they shall hold until their successors shall be appointed and qualified. The Legislature shall not have power to change the location of the State University, or the Alabama Polytechnic Institute, or the Alabama Schools for the Deaf and the Blind, or the Alabama Girls Industrial School, as now established by law, except upon a vote of two-thirds of the Legislature taken by yeas and nays and entered upon the journals.

WASHINGTON. Dec. 8. - In this discourse DR. Talmage recites some great events and shows that the world is advancing in the right direction: "Daniel ii. 3d. He will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth."

DR. Cumming—great and good man would have told us the exact time of the fulfillment of this prophecy. As I stepped into his study in London on my arrival from Paris, just after the French had surrendered at Sedan, the good doctor said to me: "It is just what I have told you about France. People laughed at me because I talked about the seven horns and the walls, but I foresaw all this from the book of Daniel and the book of Revelation." Not taking any such responsibility in the interpretation of the passage, I simply assert that there is in it suggestions of many things in our time.

Our eyes dilate and our heart quickens in its pulsations as we read of events in the third century, the sixth century, the eighth century, the fourteenth century, but there were more far-reaching events crowded into the nineteenth century than into any other, and the last twenty years eclipse any preceding twenty. We read in the daily newspapers of events announced in one paragraph and without any special emphasis—events which a Herodotus, a Josephus, a Xenophon, a Gibbon would have taken whole chapters or whole volumes to elaborate. Looking out upon our time we must cry out, in the words of the text, wonders in the heavens and in the earth.

I propose to show you that the time in which we live is wonderful for disaster and wonderful for blessing, for there must be lights and shades in this picture as in all others. Need I argue that our time is wonderful for disaster? The world has had a rough time since by the hand of God it was bowled out into space. It is an epileptic earth—convulsion after convulsion; frosts bounding it with sledge hammer of iceberg and fires melting it with furnaces seven times heated. It is a wonder to me it has lasted so long. Meteors shooting by on this side and grazing it and meteors shooting by on the other side for safety. Whole fleets and navies and argosies and flotillas of worlds sweeping all about us. Our earth like a fishing smack off the banks of Newfoundland while the Majestic and the St. Paul and the Kaiser Wilhelm der Grosse rush by. Besides that, our world has by sin been damaged in its internal machinery, and ever and anon the furnaces have burst and the walking beams of the mountains have broken, and the islands have slipped sea, and the great hulk of the world has been jarred with accidents that even and anon threatened immediate demolition.

A Century of Disasters.

But it seems to us as if the last hundred years were especially characterized by disaster—volcanic, oceanic, epidemic. I say volcanic because an earthquake is only a volcano hushed up. When Stromboli, Cotopaxi and Vesuvius stop breathing, let the foundations of the earth beware! Seven thousand earthquakes in two centuries recorded in the catalogue of the British association. Trajan, the emperor, goes to ancient Antioch and amid the splendor of his reception is met by an earthquake that nearly destroys the emperor's life. Lisbon, fair and beautiful, at 1 o'clock of the 1st of November, 1755, in six minutes, 10,000 have perished, and Voltaire writes of them, "For that region it was the last Judgment, nothing wanting but a trumpet." Europe and America feeling the throb—1,500 chimneys in Boston partly or fully destroyed.

But the disasters of other times have had their counterpart in later times. In 1817 Caracas was caught in the grip of an earthquake, in 1882 in Chile 10,000 square miles of land by volcanic force were heaved to four and seven feet of permanent elevation, in 1854 Japan felt the 20th illogical agony; Naples shaken in 1851, Mexico in 1858; Mendoza, the capital of the Argentine Republic, in 1861; Manila terrorized in 1868; the Hawaiian Islands by such force uplifted and let down in 1871; Nevada shaken in 1871, Antioch in 1872, California in 1872, San Salvador in 1873, while in 1888 what subterranean excitement, Ischia, an island of the Mediterranean, a beautiful Italian waterplace, vineyard clad, surrounded by a natural charm and historical reminiscence; yonder Capri, the summer resort of the Roman emperors; yonder Naples the paradise of art—this beautiful island suddenly topped into the trough of ill earth, 5,000 merrymakers perishing, and some of them so far down beneath the reach of human obsequies that it may be said of many a one of them, as it was said of Moses, "The Lord buried him." Italy, all Europe weeping, all Christendom weeping, where there were hearers to sympathize and Christians to pray.

But while the nations were measuring that magnitude of disaster, measuring not with golden rod like that with which the angel measured heaven, but with the black rule of death, Java of the Indian archipelago, the most fertile island of all the earth, is caught in the grip of the earthquake, and mountain after mountain goes down and city after city until that island, which produces the beverage of all the world, produced the ghastliest catastrophe. One hundred thousand people dying, dead! Coming near home, on Aug. 21, 1886 the great earthquake which frustrated one-half Charleston, S. C.

Swept by Cyclones.

But look at the disasters cyclonic. At the mouth of the Ganges are three islands, the Haitian, the Sundarbans and the Oak Shaha—in the midnight of October 1871, on all those three islands the earth was, "the waters." A cyclone arose and it rolled the sea over those three islands, end of a population of 340,000, 215,000 were drowned. Only those saved were they that had climbed to the top of the highest trees. Did you ever see a cyclone?

Then I pray God you may never see of it. I saw a cyclone on the ocean, and swept us six miles back from our course, and for thirty-six hours during the cyclone and after it we expected every man to go to the bottom. They told us before we retired at 12 o'clock that the barometer had fallen, but at 2 o'clock night we were awakened with the roar of the waves. All the lights out, and went all the lifeboats. Waters rushing through the skylights down into the cabin and down on the furnaces until we missed and smoked in the deluge. Seven hundred people praying, shrieking. One great ship poised a moment on the top, a mountain of phosphorescent fire, and then plunged down, down, down, until it seemed as if she never would again be righted. All, you never want to see a cyclone at sea.

But I was in Minnesota, where there was one of those cyclones on land that swept the city of Rochester from its foundations and took dwelling houses, barns, men, women, children, horses, cattle, a raft, tossed them into indiscriminate ruin and lifted a rail train and dashed it down, with a mightier hand than that of engineer or the airbrake.
